title: Emergency Reporting Act
official_title: To direct the Federal Communications Commission to issue reports after activation of the Disaster Information Reporting System and to make improvements to network outage reporting, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Matsui (D-CA) with Rep. Bilirakis (R-FL) and 2 cosponsors; passed the House and was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar. A bipartisan reporting-and-transparency measure on disaster communications has a reasonable path through the Senate.

votes.question: On Motion to Suspend the Rules and Pass

summary: Requires the FCC to hold hearings and publish reports on communications outages after disasters, and to study how to improve network-outage and 9-1-1 reporting.
brief: Requires FCC hearings and reports on disaster communications outages and a study of network-outage reporting.

items.main: Names the Act the “Emergency Reporting Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Reports After Activation of Disaster Information Reporting System

items.main: Requires the FCC to hold hearings and publish reports on communications outages after disasters.
items.detail: After each event lasting at least 7 days for which the FCC's Disaster Information Reporting System was activated, the Commission must hold at least one annual public hearing and, within 120 days, publish a report on the number and duration of broadband, internet-phone, and mobile outages, the users and infrastructure affected, 9-1-1 outages that block caller location or emergency calls, and resiliency recommendations. Separately, within one year the FCC must investigate and report on improving network outage reporting — including the value and burden of visual information in 9-1-1 outage notifications and outages that go unreported under current thresholds. The section grants no new FCC authority over broadband providers beyond what it specifies.

gaps: The bill requires reporting on disaster outages but does not impose any new outage-prevention or resiliency requirements on providers.
It studies unreported 9-1-1 outages but does not itself change the reporting thresholds.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Matsui
featured_quotes.text: Emergencies can happen anywhere at any time, and in those moments every second counts. When a family calls 911, they should never be met with silence. During major disasters, we have seen communications fail, and too often we are left without clear answers about what went wrong or how to prevent it from happening again. That is why I am proud to lead the Emergency Reporting Act, a bipartisan bill, with Congressman Bilirakis that helps fix this.
